en: The Mañjuśrī-ratnakara-dhāraṇī Sūtra, also titled *The Eight-Syllable Samādhi Method of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī*,
translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci.
Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
Together with a great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and immeasurable sons of the Śuddhāvāsa devas,
they surrounded him on all sides, making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, praising, and gazing up at the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One was amidst the assembly,
expounding immeasurable and wondrous dharmas of dharanis for the great multitude;
he did so further to benefit those sentient beings of meager merit in future ages.
He then entered a samādhi called "Emanating Light.
From the crown of his head, he emitted immeasurable varieties of light rays.
These rays circled around, illuminating immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds.
Having shone [upon him], the light returned and circled around the youth Mañjuśrī,
then entered the crown of his head.
Once the light had entered through the crown, it...
Mañjuśrī immediately entered a samādhi called King of Sovereignty over Dhāraṇīs.
Having entered this samādhi, he...
From his mouth, Mañjuśrī emitted immeasurable rays of light of various colors and forms;
once these rays had issued forth, they...
It then entered the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder, and [proceeded].
Placing his right knee on the ground, he joined his palms toward the Buddha,
prostrated with reverence, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
In the past, the World-Honored One spoke these words to me:
"After my Dharma has perished, during the evil age in Jambudvīpa,
Mañjuśrī will extensively benefit immeasurable sentient beings and perform the work of a Buddha."
I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and expound for me:
in what place should one dwell, and in which direction should one act so as to bring benefit?
Out of compassion and to protect all sentient beings, I pray that you will explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Mysteries, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family, that you are able to pose a question to me for the sake of all sentient beings.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
"I shall now analyze and expound this for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Mysteries,
having heard the Buddha’s words, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
Adjusting their robes and with single-minded attention, they listened.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Mysteries, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, in this Jambudvīpa, in the northeast..."
There is a country named Mahācīna.
In the center of that country is a mountain called Pañcaśīrṣa,
where the youth Mañjuśrī dwells and wanders.
He preached the Dharma therein for the sake of all sentient beings,
as well as for immeasurable and innumerable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.
Surrounding him, they made offerings and paid him homage.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the Lord Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"This is the youth Mañjuśrī."
Possessing such immeasurable majesty, supernormal powers, transformations, and sovereign adornments,
he is extensively able to benefit all sentient beings;
his power of perfected and complete merit is inconceivable.
He further addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Mañjuśrī possesses a dhāraṇī that is the most ultimate secret heart-mantra, along with the methods for painting images, constructing altars, and forming mudrās."
In the future final age when the Buddha-dharma is extinguished,
when evil dharmas increase and various calamities flourish—
at such a time as this, within Jambudvīpa in the coming world—
Beings of meager merit and little wisdom cause their evil karma to increase;
the five elements lose their order and yin and yang become disordered;
wind and rain are不调 (irregular), and malevolent stars manifest strange portents.
The gods and asuras engage in fierce battles;
the gods diminish while the asuras increase, and various calamities prevail throughout the world at such a time.
Malevolent spirits descend and transform into female forms,
inflicting various diseases upon sentient beings,
namely: throat obstructions, carbuncles, scabies, leprosy, and abdominal pains.
Malaria may recur every one, two, three, four, or even seven days; or one may suffer from diseases of wind,
bile, or phlegm, headaches, sores, swellings, eye pain, disorders of the large and small intestines, or various other ailments.
Those evil spirits and ghosts transform their bodies into various animal forms, such as insects, wolves, tigers, leopards, and lions.
Within the world, they seize sentient beings,
devouring their vital essence so that their majesty is lost and their strength declines.
At such a time, in this Jambudvīpa,
immeasurable sentient beings will meet with untimely and unjust deaths;
even if there were physicians, they would be unable to provide a cure.
Thus, in a single day of this world,
there are thirty *vimara* units.
Therefore, O Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets.
I now cause you to transmit this dharani method so that sentient beings may receive and uphold it from one another.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa—
In a single thought, they give rise to the great and virtuous aspiration for bodhicitta:
"O sons and daughters of good family, on what day shall we and all other beings be able to escape this ocean of afflictions and this prison of ignorance and craving?
Thus it is with these sons and daughters of good family.
You should protect and transform them so that their roots of goodness may increase.
You must widely disseminate this dhāraṇī so that it does not perish,
and you should always do so at the sites of the Triple Gem and before the images of the Buddha’s stūpas.
Generate the mind of right faith and prostrate with devotion.
At all times, do not neglect to diligently cultivate roots of virtue.
Train in the conduct of a bodhisattva and do not give rise to what is contrary to the Dharma.
Be filial and obedient to one's parents and respectful toward teachers and elders.
Regard all who are virtuous and good with a sense of wonder and esteem.
Constantly provide offerings of incense, flowers, and a hundred flavors of sweet delicacies morning and evening.
Do not allow yourself to become weary or indolent; instead, show respect and offer praise.
If you encounter a person who understands the Dharma, respectfully request the teachings from them.
Once you have obtained the dhāraṇī mantras, [retain them].
For seven days and seven nights, one should daily observe the eightfold precepts of the fast and recite this dhāraṇī. At that time,
the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, will take pity and mind them.

Within this Mañjuśrī-dharmakośa, there is a true Dharma,

May they obtain their heart's desires and long life;

As previously explained,
if any man or woman among the Vajra Bodhisattvas resolves their mind to recite this dhāraṇī,
they need not provide extensive offerings.
For those living at home, the various constraints and oppressions are too numerous to be fully governed by the rules; however,
if one can restrain the three types of bodily misconduct and the four types of verbal misconduct, and subdue the three delusions,
such that the ten non-virtuous actions mentioned above are forever severed at their source— this is sufficient.
One should then recite this dhāraṇī, remembering and maintaining it without forgetting.
By making offerings according to one's means and at the proper times, without deficiency or excess,
one will gradually attain accomplishment.
Except for those who harbor improper thoughts and do not give rise to the Mahāyāna bodhicitta, and those who,
toward the Triple Gem, give rise to unwholesome thoughts and commit evil deeds— for such people,
even the most minor dharmas will not be accomplished.
How much more so, then, can the Great Dharma of the Buddha be accomplished through the ritual procedures of the holy Mañjuśrī?
At that time, the Buddha spoke again to Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva:
Good son, if there are men or women who resolve their minds to recite this dhāraṇī even once,
they will immediately be able to protect themselves.
Reciting it twice can protect one's companions;
reciting it three times can provide great protection for the king.
Even Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages cannot surpass the power of this dhāraṇī.
How much less could the various minor devas, māras, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, and other evil sentient beings create obstacles?
If one recites it four times, it will immediately provide protection for one’s wife, concubines, sons, and daughters.
If recited five times, it protects all one's kinsmen and retinues;
if recited six times, it can protect all cities, towns, and villages;
if recited seven times, it can protect all sentient beings.
When one wishes to put on clothes, one should recite the mantra over them seven times;
this can eliminate all internal and external poisons as well as various calamities.
When washing the hands or face, one should recite the mantra over the water seven times.
It shall cause all sentient beings to give rise to a sense of noble reverence;
all wicked persons who see it shall be subdued,
and they themselves shall respectfully honor it and remember it day and night.
Upon seeing him, one should rejoice with a heart free from abandonment.
If a person suffers from pain in the body or its limbs and joints,
one should recite the mantra over warm water one hundred and eight times.
By bathing, one will immediately achieve healing and recovery.
If one drinks a handful of water every morning after reciting the mantra seven times,
all evil retributions within the body will be completely extinguished.
How much more so for those who are free from calamities;
furthermore, their three types of karma shall be purified and healed,
and they shall obtain a long life.
If one consecrates food and drink with this mantra, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to cause harm.
If one encounters wicked people or enemies,
one must recite this mantra.
All those enemies who give rise to malicious intentions shall naturally be subdued,
and their malice will immediately be extinguished.
One should face others with a mind of loving-kindness.
In places where there is fear, one must collect the mind;
by reciting this mantra, one will immediately be freed from all terrors.
When one wishes to lie down to sleep, one should recite this mantra one hundred and eight times;
one will then have auspicious dreams and clearly discern good and bad fortune.
If a person suffers from malaria, [one should do the same].
One who maintains this mantra should look upon the face of the person afflicted with malaria and recite it one thousand and eight times with earnest diligence;
the affliction will then be eliminated.
If one wishes to enter an army formation,
one should take ox bezoar and write this mantra upon it, wearing it on the body;
then no swords, weapons, bows, arrows, spears, or halberds shall be able to cause harm.
When entering an array for battle,
one should paint an image of the youth Mañjuśrī and place it upon an elephant or horse at the front of the three armies.
Leading the way at the front, he guides the multitude of troops;
those wicked and foolish rebels will naturally retreat and disperse.
Regarding the method for painting the image, it must be depicted with the appearance of a youth.
He rides upon a golden peacock.
If any sentient beings see this painted image, all their transgressions,
including the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, shall be completely extinguished.
They shall always have the opportunity to behold the holy youth Mañjuśrī in person and receive his direct instruction,
whereby they will immediately attain ultimate liberation and even the fruit of Buddhahood.
Throughout this interval, they shall not be associated with the deluded mind of the afflictions of the triple world.
Therefore, I exhort you to bring all sentient beings to mind.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must recite the mantra and maintain it in your memory without forgetting.
Recite it one hundred and eight times at each session, ensuring that there is no interruption.
All sentient beings who see you shall constantly come to submit and take refuge in you;
evil persons shall naturally retreat and disperse.
If one can recite this one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the day, [the benefits will be attained].
All their actions will accord with their intentions, and all their aspirations shall be fulfilled according to their hearts' desire.
Everything will be attained in complete perfection and abundance;
they shall obtain great wealth and nobility, and wherever they travel, there shall be no obstacles.
They will enjoy all manner of pleasures at their own will and ease.
Even when facing the end of life,
they will immediately behold the holy Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta manifesting his divine form before them in person.
For their sake, he expounded the profound and wondrous Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna.
Upon hearing the Dharma, their hearts were filled with great joy,
and they immediately attained the Samantamukha Samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi,
one shall be forever separated from afflictions and the cycle of birth and death;
one will then become a member of the retinue together with the holy Mañjuśrī and the great bodhisattvas.
Advancing through the stages to the third bhūmi without regression,
he dwells in the station of the noble Mañjuśrī and attains the same samādhi-gate of buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, saying:
"Good son, this is the eight-syllable dhāraṇī of great majestic power belonging to the youth Mañjuśrī."
If there are kings, princes, queens, princesses,
as well as ministers and officials, or commoners and the like,
who are able to transcribe this mantra and place it within their residence.
That family shall immediately attain great wealth and nobility, with abundant and constant riches;
their sons and daughters will be intelligent, sharp-witted, and eloquent,
possessing clever schemes and upright, handsome features.
He is beloved by all people;
whatever words he utters are honored and implemented by the multitude without contradiction.
Elephants, horses, and livestock will all flourish in great herds;
servants, slaves, treasures, and goods will be enjoyed without end;
and calamities within the household will naturally vanish.
The benevolent deities protect the house, and because the person's merit is powerful and flourishing, ghosts and spirits do not cause them affliction.
Even if there are ghosts and spirits present, they are all spirits possessing merit;
they all protect that person and do not seek out their faults.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, saying:
"Good son, this secret dhāraṇī is inconceivable;
the majestic power of all Buddhas is likewise inconceivable."
If there is anyone who can recite these eight characters of the Mahātejas Dhāraṇī,
there is furthermore a method for painting its image.
One should establish this image for the benefit of all kings who practice the ten virtuous paths.
If one is able to apply even a small amount of effort toward this dhāraṇī, one will obtain great protection;
[this applies to] all kings, princes, queens, palace attendants, and court ladies.
The hundred officials, the prime minister, and all men and women,
as well as all the people of every land—
may all their fields and houses be fully protected.
Once these images have been painted,
if anyone can install them wherever they may be,
all lands within their borders will attain peace and security.
Should there be evil bandits, water, fire, or weapons,
as well as the calamities of robbers, all shall be extinguished.
Even untimely epidemics, droughts, and floods shall be brought to an end.

Damage from insects and frost will also be entirely eliminated; the dragon kings will constantly send down rain at the proper times, so that the crops flourish and the land becomes bountiful, free from all calamities.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajra addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
regarding the extensive method for painting images which was previously expounded,"
"How should this be done? We pray that you will explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva:
"Good son, whenever one wishes to paint an image..."
First, examine the finest, high-quality cotton cloth.
One must select an auspicious day and month, a favorable lunar mansion, and the presence of benevolent planets such as Venus,
as well as a favorable hour and a propitious moment.
Thereafter, one should paint the image.
Having swept and sprinkled a pure place and smeared the ground with cow dung,
one should hang various banners and streamers, make offerings of incense and flowers, and burn aloeswood incense.
The cotton cloth must be eight cubits wide and twelve cubits long.
Upon it, one should first paint Śākyamuni Buddha,
seated upon a lotus throne made of the seven precious gems, in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
To the right of the Buddha,
paint an image of the youth Mañjuśrī,
his body adorned with necklaces and a jeweled pendant hanging from his throat.
Adorned with various exquisite garments,
the youth’s complexion was like the color of *uragasāra* gold;
kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he gazed up at the Tathāgata, assuming the posture of one requesting the Dharma.
Next, paint an image of Avalokiteśvara.
To the right of Avalokiteśvara,
paint the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Next, to the right of Samantabhadra,
paint the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Next, to the right of Ākāśagarbha, [paint...]
Paint the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
Furthermore, on the left side of Śākyamuni Buddha,
paint the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
To the left of Maitreya,
paint the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti;
to the left of Vimalakīrti, [paint...]
Paint the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
Next, to the left of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
paint the youth Candraprabha.

Next, having painted Vajrasattva on the left side of Candraprabha, these ten bodhisattvas above are each flanked by five attendants on either side; they sit upon seven-jeweled lotus flowers at their respective positions by the Buddha’s side.
All should be depicted in their original forms, including the implements held in their hands, strictly according to the original ritual manuals.
Furthermore, in the space above Śākyamuni Buddha,
one should additionally depict the Seven Buddhas.
Namely, the Tathāgata Vast Wisdom Profound Thunder-Sound King;
the Tathāgata Remover of All Obstructions;
and third, the Tathāgata Amitābha.
The Tathāgata Guṇasthāna,
the Buddha Samantagandha,
and the Buddha Duṣprasaha-vīra-garjita-caryā.
The Buddha Akṣobhya.
These seven Buddhas must all be painted in sequence;
their bodies are all golden in color.
Each [image] is like a representation of the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
In the empty spaces on both sides above each painted image,
paint one celestial being (devaputra) on each side.
Each wears a flower crown and holds a flower platter in their hands;
with one hand scattering flowers, they appear half-bodied amidst the clouds.
Their forms are upright and graceful, their bodies adorned with various ornaments.
Within the lotus pond from which Śākyamuni Buddha’s seat emerged,
two nāga kings further appeared in the pool;
one was named Nanda.
The second was named Upānanda.
These two nāga kings manifested their upper bodies from within the pond;
they had human torsos and snake heads, possessed seven heads each, and were all white in color.
His body was adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels.
To his left, the Nanda Dragon King supported the stem of the Buddha’s flower with his right hand while gazing up at the Tathāgata;
with his left hand, he held its five fingers upright.
With the thumb of his right hand, he points toward his forehead in a gesture of taking refuge.
The nāga king on the right side is identical to the one on the left. Below the youth Mañjuśrī—
Paint Maṇḍakacandragarbha, the Wrathful King,
looking up at the youth Mañjuśrī with an air of awe-struck reverence,
bowing his body as he receives instructions.
Below Maitreya Bodhisattva, paint a Dharma-holder;
do not deviate from the original hand gestures, holding an incense burner while kneeling with one leg raised,
gazing at the World-Honored One in the posture of listening to the Dharma.
On the four sides of the painted image, depict the dragon kings.
Next, paint lotuses and various exquisite flowers.
Beneath these flowers, depict Brahmā, Maheśvara, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
Next, draw four asura kings; next, draw four yakṣa-rāja luminaries.
These and those above constitute the attendants on the left side. On the right side, draw Nārāyaṇa Deva-rāja, Śakra Devendra-rāja, and the Four Great Kings.
Next, draw four Asura kings; next, draw four Yakṣa kings.
These and those above constitute the retinue on the right side; each should be depicted with its physical form according to its original appearance.
All must hold weapons in their hands without error.
Next, paint nine yakṣas holding [implements],
revealing only their upper bodies, with palms joined, facing the Buddha and gazing at the image of the Tathāgata.
Having thus explained this method for painting the image,
the Tathāgata then praised it by reciting these verses:
This method for painting this wondrous image possesses the most supreme and extraordinary merit;
all Buddhas of the three times together praise its inconceivability.
I shall now expound a small portion of the virtues of the youth Mañjuśrī.
If there are wise ones who can give rise to a single thought of mind and paint this image according to the Dharma, they shall obtain immeasurable merit and virtue,
and receive offerings and respect for all *koṭi* eons.
The four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes— All such extremely bitter and evil karmas—
By contemplating and revering the image of the Youthful One, The retributive obstacles shall all be extinguished.
Regarding whatever exists within the world, As for all classes of sentient beings who are evil:
Lacking faith in the Three Jewels, heedless and breaking the precepts,
they fear no sin; they fall into the hells,
tormented by the agonies of boiling water and fire, transmigrating through various sufferings.
Having passed through immeasurable kalpas, if one encounters this painted image and can give rise to even a single thought of joy,
gazing upon it for a brief moment or for even a fraction of an instant without distraction for a short while—
When one gives rise to a joyful mind within,
all such classes of evil karma shall be extinguished; the resulting merit will be immeasurable,
let alone for those who perform virtuous deeds and are able to cultivate pure causes.
Later, having attained excellent marks, you will possess the body of a bodhisattva,
forever gazed upon by the fourfold assembly. Always practicing with diligent vigor,
you will compassionately mind the beings in the evil realms, constantly benefiting them therein.
Running to serve as attendants, harmonizing with the light yet remaining untainted by the dust of the world,
they teach and transform others to inspire faith, leading them to liberation from the bonds of suffering.
There have been Buddhas of the past, as well as those of the present and the future.
Throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, they have all practiced the bodhisattva path,
providing bedding and entertainment, as well as elephants, horses, various precious jewels, and even their own heads,
eyes, marrow, and brains, throughout the three periods of time.
Reaching upward to the Peak of Existence and extending downward to the limits of the wind-circle,
encompassing horizontally all ten directions— all sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth who possess consciousness— I offer worship with a single mind to them all.
May nothing be done in vain; may all be provided for so that their hearts are filled with joy.
May they resolve upon the Bodhi-mind and swiftly realize the fruit of outflowlessness, attaining a state that transcends the practices of the three stages of worthiness.
Transcending the initial stages of the grounds, their merit is immeasurable;
their spiritual power is beyond compare. Though they possess such virtues, by reciting this dhāraṇī, one is able to paint an image of Mañjuśrī.
The fruit of retribution obtained by that person is such that its merit cannot be described;
even if one could know the number of grains of sand in the Ganges rivers of the ten directions,
no one could know the limit of the merit gained from painting this image.
If gods and human kings were to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
along with the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and the eight classes of beings of great majesty, making these offerings constantly throughout kalpa after kalpa;
The merit thereof is beyond calculation: whether one beholds an image of Mañjuśrī,
or is able to uphold this sutra, or day and night never forgets it,
taking flowers, incense, banners, canopies, fruits, flavors, and various foods [to offer].
And holding the seven supreme jewels, Along with spreading exquisite garments,
Without regard for months, years, or seasons, During the six periods of day and night, With sincere devotion,
never forgetting to recollect [the Buddha], One establishes these supreme offerings.
The Image of Mañjuśrī Kumāra, Holding the Eight-Character Mantra;
furthermore, from time to time, One should constantly perform prostrations and repentance before the painted image To atone for all transgressions and sins, And praise the virtues of the Great Sage.
I pray for all *siddhis*, the gateway of the Vajra-samādhi, and the fruit of the Buddha’s Bodhi;
may I be granted the realization of the six supernormal powers and swiftly awaken to the seven types of eloquence, becoming equal to Mañjuśrī and the rest.
Expounding the Dharma without end, Guiding all classes of sentient beings to reach the other shore;
May I dwell long in this world like the Great Sage, And not aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Amongst suffering sentient beings, they are born together in one place for kalpas of immeasurable length;
constantly upholding the eight-syllable dhāraṇī of the secret treasury,
they successively entrust it to one another.
Causing all to receive and uphold it, along with the mantras of various other sections,
one performs the ritual before an image of Mañjuśrī;
thus one swiftly transcends to the fruit of the Buddha-ground and further exhorts all other people.
May the eight-syllable dhāraṇī, through the single thought of sympathetic joy,
bear witness to this profound dharma-gate;
may all samādhis be like those of Mañjuśrī and the rest, and may all devas and humans [attain them].
Holding the mantra of one's own family, yet not having attained siddhi,
one should gaze upon the image of the Youth; carrying a single flower or fruit,
or perhaps a single unguent, and holding argha water in one's hands.
Kneeling on one knee, offer worship; with a sincere heart, pay respectful homage and pray for the fulfillment of your heart's desires. You shall obtain them all without doubt;
your wishes will be satisfied according to your original vows. I now address you once more.
Śrāvakas and devas, nāga kings and asuras,
the retinues of the garuḍa kings, mahoragas and other spirits,
mothers of ghosts and their kin, rākṣasas and yakṣas—
May the sovereign, minor kings, ministers, and the multitude of commoners swiftly give rise to great and expansive vows;
may they follow the tracks of Mañjuśrī’s practice and swiftly transcend to equal him in the *siddhis* of the superior, middling, and inferior grades.
May all aspirations be fulfilled; may the aspirations of all sentient beings be identical to my own.
May the habitual tendencies of all living beings be instantly extinguished, and may they ascend the precious mountain of the Buddha.
Both internal and external are entirely perfected;
One realizes the eternal, wondrous Dharmakāya and beholds the true jewel of Buddha-nature.

Like a *vajra* treasure held in the palm, one enters eternal quiescence into the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*). At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, saying:
Within this Eight-Syllable Mahātejas Dhāraṇī Method,
there is a secret, most excellent, and inconceivable ritual for the maṇḍala and mudrās;
it is the most extensive and supreme among all dharmas.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, good men, or good women who,
in accordance with the Dharma, uphold, recite, read, transcribe, and practice it,
they will achieve all auspiciousness in this present life.
All their undertakings will be fulfilled and their lifespan will be long;
they will be loved and respected by all people, who will regard them with deep veneration.
After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the heavens to enjoy immeasurable bliss.
Or they may be born into royal palaces in positions of honor,
enjoying wealth and happiness with bodies free from the suffering of illness;
they attain the knowledge of past lives and have diminished greed, hatred, and delusion.
He understood cause and effect well and held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem.
Although he inherited a noble position, his mind was free from arrogance;
due to the powerful force of past causes, he devoted himself to the study and recitation of the Mahāyāna.
Compassionate toward all beings with a mind free from competitiveness, they constantly benefit sentient beings.
If born among humans of lower status, they will be noble, wealthy, distinguished, and handsome;
their proclamations will be eloquent and sharp, and they will be beloved by others.
During their long lifespans, they will be free from calamities and misfortunes;
no one shall violate the trust of their aspirations or the intentions of their hearts.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, regarding that which you previously spoke concerning this Dharma—
namely, the secret maṇḍala ritual— what are its particulars?
We pray that you, who know the future, will explain it in detail for us."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajra, saying:
"Excellent! Sons and daughters of good family who, having conceived a mind of faith and reverence, perform the rite of constructing a maṇḍala."
First, one must select a pure, excellent, and superior site.
Once the site has been obtained,
it must all be deeply excavated to remove tiles, rubble, bricks, stones, thorns, hair, ash, husks, excrement, and other impurities.
Having removed all impure substances, take good, pure earth and firmly compact it until it is level.
Then, measure out that ground according to the four directions: east, west, south, and north.
One should properly measure eight cubits or four cubits.
Taking fragrant water, one should smear the ground to make it bright and clean.
Then, one takes cow dung and mixes it with fragrant water.
Furthermore, smear the ground three times.
Then, take thick fragrant water and sprinkle it upon the altar site.
Next, take a white cord and measure out eight cubits.
Measure the ground according to its dimensions in the four directions— east, west,
south, and north— and mark the lengths with powder-dots.
Distribute the altar precincts to form three tiers.
Open gates on all four sides.
Measure and establish the boundaries so that they are neither too wide nor too narrow.
Only then should the five-colored powders be applied to the boundary positions.
In all methods for painting the mandala and the arrangement of ritual implements and mudrās,
one always begins from the eastern side.
First, one paints the five-crested mudrā.
Next, draw the seal of the utpala lotus.
Next, draw the seal of the fangs.
Next, draw the seal of the face of the youth Mañjuśrī.
Next, having drawn the spear seal (śakti-mudrā), draw the aforementioned five seals on the eastern side within the mandala.
Next, draw the lotus seal (padma-mudrā). Next, draw the utpala flower seal.
Next, draw the banner seal (dhvaja-mudrā).
Next, draw the banner seal.
Next, draw the parasol.
Next, draw the gate with a bird-head finial.
Next, draw the wheel-mark of the chariot.
Next, draw the auspicious mark of Kabaṃsipa.
Next, draw the peacock mark.
Next, draw a white elephant;
next, draw a horse;
next, draw a humpbacked ox.
Next, draw a water buffalo;
next, draw a black ram;
next, draw a white sheep.
Next, draw the human figures;
next, draw the youths. All the aforementioned mudrās must be drawn clearly and in sequence outside the gate. Thus are the three types of maṇḍalas.
Outside the outer precinct of the maṇḍala, further draw the yakṣa generals.
In the east, one should paint the yakṣa general named Maṇibhadra;
in the south, the yakṣa general named Pūrṇabhadra.
Next, paint the yakṣa general named Virūpākṣa in the west.
Next, paint the yakṣa general.
The Sanskrit name for the King Vaiśravaṇa is the North.
As with the four generals above, each dwells in his own direction,
presiding over the four sides of the maṇḍala and leading the various spirits and deities to protect their respective quarters.
Next, draw the sun and moon; next, draw the seven stars;
next, draw the twenty-eight lunar mansions; and next, draw the goddess Haritī and the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī).
These are as described above.
The forms, implements, and mudrās drawn outside the mandala must all be depicted strictly according to the ritual rules;
do not allow them to be disordered or erroneous.
The methods for applying colors have thus been fully explained.
If practitioners of the path follow these regulations, they will surely achieve their goals through diligent cultivation and application of their practice; there shall be no error or failure.
Furthermore, according to another method, if one is performing the rite for Rāśa,
one should practice within a clean dwelling.
If one wishes to seek a white elephant, [one should proceed as follows].
If one goes to an elephant stable and performs the rite there, one will surely obtain one's original vow.
If one wishes to seek a horse,
and performs the rite in a horse stable, one will surely obtain one's original vow.
If one is bitten by a snake,
one may perform the rite at a great pond where there is a nāga.
If one suffers from malaria lasting from one day up to seven days, [the same applies].
If one performs the rite at the southern edge of one's own village, hamlet, or dwelling, one will be cured.
However, if one is possessed by a malevolent spirit (*bhūta*) or a *rākṣasa*,
one should perform the rite in an empty room or in a cemetery (*śmaśāna*).
The affliction will then be eliminated and healed.
If one is possessed by a piśāca spirit,
one should perform the rite beneath a kovidāra tree.
Their affliction shall be immediately cured and healed.
If one is possessed by any spirits, ghosts, or *uṣmanaka* (heat-demons),
one should go to the room where a corpse lies.
Or one may perform it in the room where a newborn child is born.
If someone has been struck by various poisons,
one should recite this eight-character mantra over water seven times.
If one gives it for them to drink, they will immediately be cured.
If there are animals afflicted by an epidemic,
one should perform the rite beneath a fruit tree, and the epidemic will be eliminated.
If one desires that the crops in one's fields be lush, abundant, and yield a full harvest,
one should perform this rite within a garden or grove, and one’s wishes will be fulfilled. Furthermore,
if there is a woman afflicted by various malignant diseases, [she shall be cured].
If one is afflicted by ghosts, spirits, garuḍas, gandharvas,
or others who have siphoned off human vital essence to cause diseases or rashes,
one should perform [the rite] by a riverbank or upon a mountain peak.
All such spirits and deities shall keep their distance;
his body will be restored to health, and thereafter he shall be free from all calamities and misfortunes,
even if he has been afflicted by any *ḍākinī* spirits.
One should perform the rite in a secluded and quiet place or by the side of flowing water;
the spirit will then depart from that person, and no further afflictions or calamities will arise.
These ritual procedures should be performed during the height of midday or at midnight.
When the ritual is about to conclude and one wishes to dismantle the altar,
one should recite the eight-character mantra.
The items within the altar should be cast into water or given to the poor.
Thereafter, all matters sought were fully accomplished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The power of this great dhāraṇī is unspeakable."
If a person constantly upholds this, they can eliminate all illnesses;
whatever activities they undertake will all be perfectly fulfilled,
and they shall attain a long life, provided they behold this maṇḍala.
All sins shall be utterly extinguished; if one seeks worldly happiness,
wealth, nobility, and sovereign power, or if one grows weary of worldly desires and seeks birth beyond death, one shall transcend the ocean of all suffering.
Training in the conduct of enlightenment To subdue all the hosts of Māras,
Whoever enters this maṇḍala Will surely attain great power.

At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata [spoke].
He addressed the Bodhisattva Vajra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Since you are now able to gather in all sentient beings, you have given rise to this great mind and are extensively capable of practicing deeds of great benefit."
"Good son, I now entrust this Dharma into the hands of Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma,
so that in future ages within Jambudvīpa,
it may be widely proclaimed and disseminated for the sake of sentient beings."
The youth Mañjuśrī, right there before the Buddha, leaped for joy with exuberance;
with a serene and smiling countenance, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we have now received [this teaching] from the Tathāgata in the midst of this great assembly."
"You entrust me with this *dhāraṇī* Dharma-treasury Sūtra;
I shall protect it and I shall uphold it in the evil age after the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa."
He caused all sentient beings to receive and uphold it according to the Dharma,
to propagate it widely, and to ensure it was never interrupted.
Thus, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma,
Immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who hear this Dharma shall all be freed from sorrow and affliction;
immeasurable sentient beings will resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra,
the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, and the eight classes of beings,
including devas, nāgas, and spirits, [all rejoiced].
With one voice they praised the Tathāgata Śākyamuni for being able to preach this Dharma, exclaiming, "Excellent!
How rare! This has never been heard before.
Prostrating at the Buddha's feet, they rejoiced with leaping joy and resolved to practice it with single-minded devotion.
